title: Thermophysical properties of high density polyethylene and phase change materials: a systematic study on the evaluation of specific heat capacity and thermal diffusivity
abstract: Abstract The testing and optimization of parameters for the direct measurement of specific heat capacity and thermal diffusivity of organic substances in the range of temperature 5–90 °C were investigated. High density polyethylene (HDPE) was selected as widely studied thermoplastic polymer due to its well-known thermophysical properties available in literature. Eicosane (C20), an oligomer selected as a pure substance, and a fatty acid mixture (SA) representing a commercial phase change material (PCM) were also investigated due to the fundamental importance of characterizing the thermophysical properties of PCMs to model their thermal behavior and implement their use in practical applications. After a preliminary analysis on the influence of scanning rate on the PCM phase transition via Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC), identifying 1 °C min −1  as the optimal rate to balance thermal inertia and enthalpy accuracy, we determined the best parameters for specific heat capacity determined by comparing the sapphire method and the TOPEM ®  technique. Subsequently we compared the thermal diffusivity determined using Laser Flash Analysis (LFA) and the Hot Disk (transient plane heat source) method, evidencing that specific geometric arrangements, such as specimen thickness, are critical for ensuring result convergence. The study highlights the inverse temperature dependence of specific heat capacity and thermal diffusivity, confirming the phase transition as a region of thermophysical indetermination where property values lack physical significance. We propose a critical discussion regarding different strategies and parameters, stressing that cross-technique validation is essential to overcome methodological concerns and achieve the high degree of accuracy required for reliable predictive modeling in thermal energy storage.
journal: Journal of Thermal Analysis and Calorimetry

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The knowledge of accurate thermal properties represents a fundamental requirement in all those applications where heat transfer processes significantly impact the realistic estimation of the profitability, energy savings, costs, and operational assessments [ 1 ,  2 ]. In this context, the availability of accurate databases for thermal diffusivity, specific heat and thermal conductivity is strategic for characterizing the thermal behavior of materials during thermal power exchanges, particularly in the transient regimes typical of charge and discharge cycles. Among these, thermal diffusivity is a fundamental parameter not only in heat transfer analysis, but also for designing procedures involving high-performance materials, such as Phase Change Materials (PCMs). These materials are expected to have a significant impact on applications related to thermal energy storage (TES) and management [ 3 ], provided that their thermophysical properties are determined with the high degree of accuracy and low uncertainty required for reliable predictive modeling.

The measurement of thermal diffusivity is a challenging task since it is achieved by solving the differential heat transfer equation based on temperature variations induced by a time-varying heat flux applied to a suitable sample [ 4 ,  5 ]. Since this approach pertains to a class of inverse problems [ 6 ], the resulting thermal properties are obtained through numerical models that are strongly sensitive to the accuracy of the experimental quantities used for computation. These, in turns, are affected by parameters such as sample preparation, calibration, and the accuracy degree of the experimental operative procedures. Several commercially available technologies are usually employed to determine this property for different kinds of materials. Among these, methods that have reached a consolidated and recognized commercial maturity are the Hot Wire [ 7 ,  8 ] and the Hot Disk techniques [ 9 ]. The latter, based on the analysis of the response function of a hot sensor arranged between identical specimens, is one of the techniques employed to determine the thermal diffusivity of the materials investigated in this work. The other adopted methodology is the Laser Flash Analysis (LFA) [ 10 ,  11 ], a non-contact technique through which the thermal diffusivity is directly determined. Laser interferometers and photothermal methods [ 12 ,  13 ] are further innovative alternatives that require, however, complex and expensive instrumentations. Regardless of the method, obtaining reliable measurements requires careful sample preparation and significant operator experience. In recent years, sophisticated techniques involving microwave heating [ 14 ] and the quasi-steady-state Ångstrom technique [ 15 ] have also been investigated for specific applications. Thermal diffusivity is a critical property since, together with specific heat and density values determined under identical conditions, it allows the determination of thermal conductivity. Consequently, both thermal diffusivity and specific heat are reference properties for the characterization of material thermal behavior. For this reason, it was deemed appropriate to measure both during the same experimental campaign to ensure consistency and reduce the uncertainties associated with varying thermal histories. However, as demonstrated by the results of this investigation, thermal diffusivity measurements obtained with different techniques can sensibly diverge due to methodological sensitivities [ 16 ].

Focusing on specific heat capacity ( c p ) measurements, Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) is the most conventional technique widely used for the thermal characterization of materials, specifically for the measurement of their specific heat. In recent years, the experimental techniques developed for the measurement of this property via DSC have experienced significant technological advancements [ 17 ]. Initially, the “direct method” provided rough estimations of the heat capacity by simply dividing the heat flow by the sample mass and the heating rate. A more accurate strategy consisted in the “steady state” method using an Alternating Differential Scanning Calorimetry (ADSC), or Temperature-Modulated Differential Scanning Calorimetry (TMDSC), in which the sample is subjected to periodic heating and, once a dynamic equilibrium is reached, the software can evaluate the specific heat capacity applying the same principle as the direct method. However, while both mentioned methods often provide poor accuracy, significant improvements can be achieved using the “sapphire method.” It consists of a comparison of the heat flux obtained scanning the investigated sample with that obtained subjecting a sapphire (α-Al 2 O 3 ) reference of known specific heat capacity to the same thermal ramp. Nowadays, the sapphire method is probably the most adopted strategy and it can be easily followed according to the ASTM E1269-11 standard, which carefully describes the procedure [ 18 ]. However, its accuracy remains highly dependent on the choice of scanning rate and meticulous baseline subtraction. An evolution in the use of modulated techniques consisted of the superimposition of a sinusoidal temperature variation to the linear thermal ramp, to permit the distinction of reversible and non-reversible phenomena by deconvolution of the total heat [ 19 ]. Initially, this method also required a calibration curve, as in the sapphire method, but more recently, the direct evaluation has become possible thanks to software refinements [ 20 ,  21 ]. An advanced technique in TMDSC is the Temperature-modulated Order-based Parameter Estimation Method (TOPEM ® ), patented in 2005 by Mettler Toledo (Greifensee, Switzerland) and whose working principles were detailed by Schawe et al. [ 22 ]. It is based on stochastic temperature modulation, consisting of the overlay of a ramped temperature with a time series of stochastic temperature pulses of different durations, permitting the direct determination of the quasi-static heat capacity deriving from the reversing heat flow signal.

Two different kinds of material have been chosen for this experimental study: a polymer such as high density polyethylene (HDPE), a reference and widely studied material due to its exceptional chemical properties and technological performances for which, furthermore, extensive and consolidated thermophysical properties databases are available both in open literature and manuals. This choice allows for a stable benchmark to verify the accuracy of the measurements against established literature values, enabling a critical evaluation of the performances of the equipment used; restricting the field of organic materials, a class of emerging interest is that of PCMs, whose thermophysical properties are still limited in literature and the experimental procedures usually adopted for their measurements not yet well consolidated. Organic PCMs, including paraffins like eicosane (C20) and fatty acid mixtures like stearic–palmitic acid (SA), are nowadays particularly attractive due to their high latent heat, making them ideal candidates for TES and passive thermal regulation applications [ 23 ,  24 – 25 ]. Therefore, the definition of reliable procedures for the determination of PCM thermal properties is a strategic goal. Despite these expectations, many detailed works regarding PCMs neglect the thermophysical properties determination [ 26 ,  27 – 28 ] or their temperature dependence [ 29 ,  30 ]. Moreover, they have been often investigated by using non-conventional characterization techniques [ 31 ]. Among them, the Temperature-history method [ 32 ,  33 ] or evolutions like the Peltier-element-based Adiabatic Scanning Calorimeter (pASC) [ 34 ] were studied showing promising results. However, no standardized equipment implementing these methods is present on the market, limiting their use to laboratory scale. Despite their importance, the application of well-established procedures for measuring thermal properties for a wide range of materials and conditions, currently represents a challenging task. In this context, this work aims to propose some experimental approaches widely applied for the determination of the two investigated properties, aiming to highlight the following aspects:

to investigate the impact of testing parameters on both heat capacity and thermal diffusivity. These properties have been systematically determined for the selected materials within the temperature range 5–90 °C; regarding PCMs, a detailed experimental campaign has been dedicated to evaluate how the choice of the DSC scanning rate affects the phase transition temperature range, confirming how the selection of this parameter for operating the measurement procedure is still a topic of debate [ 35 ]. By crossing the phase transition, the properties both for the solid and liquid phase have been determined, considering that, for PCMs, systematic studies on both phases are yet limited, focusing the interest limitedly to phase transition temperature determination; by covering different testing conditions, an extended effort has been carried on specific heat analysis to compare the measurements obtained by the sapphire method and by the TOPEM ®  technique; an extended part of this study is dedicated to a critical discussion on the thermal diffusivity values obtained by Laser Flash Analysis (LFA) and Hot Disk (Transient Plane heat Source method), evidencing both the potentialities and the criticalities of these apparatuses and the reliability of the obtained results.

Further critical issues emerged during this experimental campaign are adequately discussed in the corresponding sections of the manuscript. Specifically, this pertains to experimental protocols such as differences in calibration accuracy versus precision, sensitivity, and sample geometry or masses. Other topics focus on a critical analysis as the choice of the suggested operating conditions that, mainly, must be selected after appropriate tests conducted knowledgeably by the operator without having a specific support from the provided guidelines that, often, are inaccurate or contradictory.

Consequently, this study proposes a systematic comparative approach involving distinct methodologies and instruments as a robust pathway to overcome the inherent complexities in characterizing these significant thermophysical properties.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: The thermoplastic polymer selected as widely studied material of known thermophysical properties was High Density Polyethylene (HDPE) PLASTENE ®  AD25, provided by Poliplast S.p.A. (Casnigo, Italy). This specific grade (PLASTENE ®  AD25) was selected to serve as a reliable benchmark for the experimental setup. It was supplied in the form of fine powder of density 0.955 g cm −3  and melt flow index (MFI) of 25 g 10 min −1  (at 190 °C, 2.16 kg).

Two organic Phase Change Materials (PCMs) were selected for this systematic study. First, a commercial product of less controlled composition, representing typical substances utilized in real applications was investigated. A palmitic and stearic acid mixture (SA) was chosen, commercially known as “Fatty acids C16-18”, provided by Carlo Erba Reagents (Val De Ruil, France). Its declared melting point is 55 °C and the density is 0.890 g cm −3  at 20 °C.

The second PCM was selected as a pure paraffin to analyze a substance of well-controlled composition. The choice was oriented to eicosane (C20) of purity > 99%, provided by Merck KGaA (Darmstadt, Germany). The producer declared a melting interval of 35–37 °C, and density of 0.789 g cm −3  at 20 °C. The chemical identification of all investigated materials is summarized in Table  1 . sections.heading: Sample preparation
paragraphs: HDPE was melt compounded at 135 °C for 10 min using a Thermo Haake 600 melt compounder (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) equipped with counter-rotating rotors at a fixed speed of 50 rpm. The material was subsequently hot pressed at 140 °C for 5 min into a Carver (Wabash, IN, USA) press equipped with steel molds of the desired specimen shape.

The PCMs were tested as provided or heated above their complete melting and casted into steel or polytetrafluoroethylene molds of the desired geometry. The surfaces were polished at room temperature when presented roughness and imperfections.

sections.heading: Experimental technologies
paragraphs: Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) was performed with a Mettler DSC5 + calorimeter (Mettler Toledo, Greifensee, Switzerland). Different thermal cycles were performed using 40 µl aluminum crucibles and specimen masses near 10 mg determined with an analytical balance (uncertainty ± 0.1 mg), under a nitrogen flux of 100 mL min⁻ 1 . The heat flux and tau lag calibrations were carried out with indium, yielding a measured melting enthalpy of 28.81 ± 0.01 J g −1  (ref: 28.70 ± 1.00 J g −1 ). A three-point temperature calibration was performed using distilled water (measured: 0.15 ± 0.02 °C; ref: 0.00 ± 0.50 °C), indium (measured: 156.7 ± 0.1 °C; ref: 156.60 ± 0.30 °C), and zinc (measured: 419.3 ± 0.1 °C; ref: 419.50 ± 0.70 °C), confirming the instrument operates well within admitted tolerances.

First, single heating ramps were imposed to investigate the effect of the scanning rate in the phase transitions. Heating rates from 10 to 0.01 °C min −1  were imposed to identify the optimal balance between thermal inertia and signal resolution. The relevant values extrapolated from the curves were the temperature of the melting peak ( T peak ), the range of the phase transition ( ΔT m ) and the melting enthalpy ( ΔH m ). The PCMs were then subjected to a thermal cycle of heating–cooling–heating at the optimized rate of ± 1 °C min −1 , from 25 to 65 °C, aimed to simulate the working condition after resetting the thermal history of the material. The peak phase transition temperature ( T m1 ,  T c  and  T m2 ) and the corresponding enthalpies ( ΔH m1 ,  ΔH c , and  ΔH m2 ) were evaluated from the curves.

The specific heat capacity ( c p ) was evaluated from 10 °C to 95 °C for HDPE and SA, while for C20 the range was restricted to 5–65 °C. In all tests the specific heat capacity was evaluated every 5 °C and values are reported as the mean value and standard deviation of three specimens. Reference and sample crucibles were selected with a mass difference < 0.05 mg to minimize baseline offsets; no lid was applied, and a blank curve subtraction was performed. Optimal PCM contact with the crucible was guaranteed by delicately pushing the sample with a Teflon rod onto the bottom of the crucible. The specific heat capacity was first determined by comparison with a sapphire reference following the ASTM E1269-11 standard [ 18 ] adopting scanning rates of 0.1, 1, 5 and 10 °C min −1 . Then, the specific heat capacity was determined with the TOPEM ®  technique to evaluate the impact of stochastic modulation at 1 °C min −1  (pulse height of 0.1 °C) and 0.3 °C min −1  (pulse height of 0.05 °C). For C20, an additional rate of 0.1 °C min −1  was explored (pulse height of 0.05 °C). The selected pulse width was 15–30 s in all the cases.
The evaluation was carried out adopting a width of calculation window of 120 s, a shift of calculation window of 10 s, and a width of smoothing window of 200 s.

Thermal diffusivity was evaluated by using a Laser Flash Analyzer (LFA) NETZSCH LFA 446 (Selb, Germany). HDPE specimens were disks of 12.7 mm diameter and thickness of 2 and 2.5 mm, with the latter chosen to optimize the signal-to-noise ratio. PCMs were tested by using two different sample holders: a standard holder for solid-phase disks, and a specialized “low viscosity liquid” holder where the PCM is contained between two stainless steel plates. Three specimens for each sample were tested with 5 shots every 5 °C, from 15 to 90 °C for HDPE and SA, and from 5 to 55 °C for C20. All LFA measurements utilized a laser voltage of 250 V and a pulse width of 0.6 ms. To ensure that the temperature rise remained within the linear range of the infrared detector, a signal amplification factor between 400 and 700 was employed, utilizing the software’s "Optimize Gain" automatic adjustment feature shot-by-shot. The analysis maximized the  R 2  fit by selecting the “Transparent” model for HDPE, the “Layers model” for the specialized holder for low viscosity liquids, and the “Standard” method for solid PCM disks.

The validity of the obtained diffusivities was verified independently using a Hot Disk thermal analyzer equipped with a 7577 sensor (diameter of 4.002 mm), following the ISO 22007 standard [ 36 ]. The apparatus was placed into a Memmert HCP climatic chamber to control the temperature, imposing a constant relative humidity of 30%. HDPE was tested at 15, 30 and 45 °C, whereas C20 at 10, 20, and 45 °C and SA at 15 and 30 °C. Solid specimens were plates of thickness 10 mm, while C20 at the liquid state was tested by immersing the sensor directly into the molten PCM within a beaker, adopting a configuration similar to that exploited by Zhong et al. [ 37 ]. The measure for the molten SA was not possible for the limited reachable temperature from the sensor and the climatic chamber. Signals of 15 mW were applied for 20 to 40 s, and diffusivity was calculated in the range 50–200 acquired points. Results are reported as mean value ± standard deviation of three measurements.

sections.heading: Approach to thermal analysis
paragraphs: The evaluation of the thermophysical properties of materials is not trivial and conceals many issues, primarily their strong dependence on temperature [ 38 ]. Consequently, this necessitates a refined DSC calibration for the specific heat capacity determination, adopting at least two reference materials to adequately cover the entire temperature range under investigation, and restricting the admitted tolerances in either temperature or enthalpy. As demonstrated in our calibration phase, while the repeatability of reference materials is often high, achieving absolute accuracy remains a significantly more complex challenge than ensuring precision. Moreover, the determination of this property requires a skilled and highly trained operator, who must manage careful sample preparation, take precise note of the mass, and ensure proper contact between specimen and crucible, selecting crucibles of a mass as similar as possible (suggested difference < 0.05 mg). Notwithstanding all the steps being conducted carefully, the obtained values often result uncertain, with high deviation and scarce repeatability.

This relationship confirms the temperature dependence and highlights that associations between heat capacity values and temperatures are not always respected. Crucially, during a phase transition, the specific heat capacity has no physical meaning by definition because, according to Eq. ( 1 ), it tends toward infinity; thus, the melting region constitutes a zone of thermophysical indetermination and uncertainty. Moreover, the transition phenomena in DSC are heavily affected by the scanning rate due to thermal lag and thermal inertia. Likewise, the measured specific heat capacity is affected by the scanning rate in DSC measurements.

Regarding emerging strategies for  c p  evaluation, the TOPEM ®  technique has been often used for second-order transition detection, e.g., Fraga et al., who extensively compared the different testing parameters in cooling an amorphous polymer to determine the glass transitions [ 39 ]. However, notwithstanding 20 years of use ,  testing parameters are not yet well-established for the accurate determination of specific heat capacity in organic materials. Table  2  summarizes the adopted testing parameters in a selection of remarkable studies exploring the TOPEM ®  technique, alongside the suggested parameters provided by the producers. Table 2 TOPEM ®  parameters adopted in remarkable studies Material Temperature/°C Scanning rate/°C min −1 Pulse height/°C Pulse width/s References Polycarbonate (PC) 180–80 0.02–2 0.002–0.2 15–30 [ 39 ] Epoxy resin 25–125 0.015–0.1 0.1 15–30 [ 40 ,  41 ] Polyvinyl chloride (PVC)–montmorillonite (MMT) 30–85 2 0.5 15–30 [ 42 ] Phenol copolymer 18–57 0.5 0.5 15–30 [ 43 ] Polyethylene glycol (PEG)–methacrylate copolymers 10–50 0.25 0.0005 30–60 [ 44 ] Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) 32–36 0.1–0.5 0.1–0.3 n.d [ 45 ] Inorganic PCM (Al-Cu-Si alloy) 100–700 1 n.d n.d [ 46 ] Epoxy resin 0–270 2 1 15–30 [ 47 ] Metallic glass -50–550 2 1 15–30 [ 48 ] “Normal measurements” n.d 0.5–2 0.002–1 15–30 Suggested by Mettler Toledo [ 49 ] “High precision with frequency evaluation” n.d  ≤ 0.5 1 (For melting ≤ 0.1–0.002) 15–30 Suggested by Mettler Toledo [ 49 ] n.d. = not declared

From Table  2  emerges a wide variety of possible scanning rates and pulse heights, demonstrating that producer guidelines leave room for different interpretations. Significantly, there is a persistent lack of reported information regarding the evaluation parameters, such as calculation width and the window shift, which hinders the reproducibility of stochastic modulation results.

As anticipated, a typical approach is the determination of thermal conductivity after the independent direct measurement of these three quantities, as in the case of the LFA, which directly measures only diffusivity. In contrast, the Hot Disk method recursively determines both thermal diffusivity and conductivity, as the former is needed to define the characteristic time required for the expression of the latter [ 36 ]. Comparing the two techniques, the laser flash method is more user-friendly and enables automated evaluation at multiple temperatures without continuous operator intervention. However, it is extremely sensitive to sample geometry, requiring perfectly parallel and smooth surfaces, precisely controlled thickness, and accurate positioning in the holder. Conversely, the Hot Disk offers more freedom in sample preparation, requiring only two smooth surfaces to clamp the sensor and a specimen thickness greater than the probing depth [ 36 ]. Nevertheless, the selection of testing parameters for Hot Disk is critical, as is the temperature control, necessitating a climatic chamber for the entire setup. Consequently, extended stabilization periods are necessary to reach thermal equilibrium, and measurements are frequently restricted to temperatures close to ambient. For this reason, in this work, Hot Disk measurements were conducted only at selected temperatures to cross-validate the LFA values. This comparison is essential because methodological divergence is quite common in thermophysical characterization [ 16 ].

In the following sections, the influence of the DSC scanning rate on first-order transition analysis is examined. The focus then shifts to the specific heat capacity determination, investigating the influence of testing parameters in the conventional sapphire method compared to TOPEM ® , evidencing how this property is strongly influenced by the temperature. Finally, thermal diffusivity is evaluated as a function of temperature via LFA and Hot Disk, highlighting the technical precautions required for precise and reliable measurements.

sections.heading: First-order transition determination
paragraphs: Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) is the primary characterization technique for evaluating first-order transition. In this section, a preliminary investigation into the effect of the scanning rate on the melting transition is performed, comparing results across heating rates ranging from 0.01 °C min −1  to 10 °C min −1 . Subsequently, the complete DSC cycle of heating–cooling-heating on the PCMs is presented at the refined scanning rate of 1 °C min −1 .

sections.heading: Influence of the heating rate
paragraphs: The curves illustrating the influence of the scanning rate on the phase transitions are reported in Fig.  1 , while Tables  3 – 5  list the characteristics melting parameters. Fig. 1 DSC scanning rate effect on melting:  a  HDPE;  b  SA;  c  C20. The amplification of the heat flux necessary to compare the peaks at the different rates are reported near the corresponding curve Table 3 Melting features in DSC as function of scanning rate for HDPE Rate/°C min −1 T peak /°C Δ T m /°C Δ H m /J g −1 10 134.9 95.4–148.9 185.9 1 129.5 108.6–132.5 174.0 0.1 129.3 119.8–132.2 155.7 T peak  = melting temperature peak;  ΔT m  = melting temperature range;  ΔH m  = melting enthalpy Table 4 Melting features in DSC as function of scanning rate for SA Rate/°C min −1 T peak /°C Δ T m /°C Δ H m /J g −1 10 60.2 36.6–72.0 220.8 1 58.3 46.1–59.7 210.1 0.1 57.6 53.9–58.1 169.4 0.01 57.5 56.0–58.1 153.2 T peak  = melting temperature peak;  ΔT m  = melting temperature range;  ΔH m  = melting enthalpy Table 5 Melting features in DSC as function of scanning rate for C20 Rate/°C min −1 T peak /°C Δ T m /°C Δ H m /J g −1 10 41.1 27.5–51.0 230.9 1 37.5 29.5–39.1 229.3 0.1 36.5 33.4–36.9 219.8 0.01 36.3 35.3–36.4 188.4 T peak  = melting temperature peak;  ΔT m  = melting temperature range;  ΔH m  = melting enthalpy

As observed, high scanning rates induce significant "tau lag" and thermal inertia, while ultra-low rates successfully narrow the melting temperature range but result in a systematic underestimation of the melting enthalpy. Specifically, a rate of 10 °C min −1 , though the most adopted for DSC tests, does not permit a clear correspondence of the melting phenomenon with temperature. This is evidenced by both the broadening of the melting range and a significant peak shift toward higher temperatures. This indicates that the tau lag calibration performed on Indium is not sufficient to compensate for the thermal inertia of highly endothermic phenomena, such as the phase transition of polymers or oligomers, which can be an order of magnitude higher in enthalpy than the metal references used for heat flux calibration. Decreasing the scanning rate restricts the melting interval, particularly by anticipating the end temperature. However, a physical limit exists; a single melting temperature cannot be defined in organic materials due to a molecular weight distribution, a phenomenon more evident in HDPE than in the PCMs. Thus, while the melting interval can be restricted to 1–2 °C for PCMs and 12 °C for HDPE at rates of 0.1–0.01 °C min −1 , these materials differ fundamentally from metals, where the onset corresponds to the melting of the entire crystal lattice. While these ultra-low rates such as 0.01 °C min −1  are more representative of many real-world PCM applications [ 50 ], they introduce significant measurement challenges. A similar systematic study was conducted by the authors in a previous work on SA using a DSC30 (Mettler Toledo) yielding comparable results; however, with the current DSC5 + , the baseline at 0.1 °C min −1  appears significantly less noisy. This evidences the evolution of the calorimetry technology [ 51 ], as the newer model permits acceptable resolution even at 0.01 °C min −1 .

Despite this technological progress, the melting enthalpy values remain significantly affected by the heating rate, with a progressive reduction of measured enthalpy observed at the low scanning rates, as evidenced by Fatahi et al. [ 35 ]. This decrease in the total enthalpy, observed when reducing the scanning rate from 20 to 2 °C min −1 , has also been documented in other exothermic phenomena, such as the crosslinking of epoxy resins, where reaction enthalpies dropped from 158 to 102 J g −1  [ 47 ]. It must be strongly emphasized that since the heat flux of the DSC is standardly calibrated at 10 °C min −1  (preferentially using Indium), the use of excessively low scanning rates should be critically examined, as they could systematically modify the registered enthalpy and affect the reliability of the thermal characterization. These findings align with existing literature. For instance, Saeed et al. identified a compromise at 3 °C min −1  [ 52 ], while Valentini et al. found the best scanning rate of 1 °C min −1  to thermally characterized organic PCMs [ 53 ]. These results have been corroborated by other authors who have ascertained and evaluated a speed of 0.5–2 °C min −1  for the accurate characterization of the melting phase transition [ 54 ,  55 – 56 ]. Following both literature and own experimental findings, the authors conclude that 1 °C min −1  is the optimum scanning rate to appreciate the temperature of the phase transition with sufficient precision without underestimating the melting enthalpy and without exceeding the testing time.

sections.heading: Melting and crystallization of PCM
paragraphs: The curves of the neat PCMs at the refined scanning rate of 1 °C min −1  during a cycle of melting-crystallization-melting are shown in Fig.  2 , representing the first heating (a), cooling (b), and second heating (c) scans. Table  6  reports the characteristic parameters of the first-order transitions derived from the curves. Fig. 2 Curves of DSC at 1 °C min −1 :  a  first heating;  b  cooling;  c  second heating Table 6 Melting and crystallization temperatures and enthalpies of PCMs from DSC at 1 °C min −1 Sample T m1 / °C ΔH m1 /J g −1 T c /°C ΔH c /J g −1 T m2 /°C ΔH m2 /J g −1 C20 37.5 229 34.1 227 37.3 230 SA 59.0 194 54.7 190 58.6 194 T m1  = melting peak temperature during the first heating scan;  ΔH m1  = specific melting enthalpy during the first heating scan;  T c  = crystallization peak temperature during cooling;  ΔH c  = specific crystallization enthalpy during cooling;  T m2  = melting peak temperature during the second heating scan;  ΔH m2  = specific melting enthalpy during the second heating scan

Eicosane shows a double crystallization peak, a typical feature in paraffins [ 57 ,  58 – 59 ]. The second sharper peak is often attributed to a solid–solid phase transition to a more ordered molecular configuration, a phenomenon introduced by Craig et al. in 1967 [ 60 ]. An alternative interpretation suggests a two-step process: the initial crystallization of a more mobile molecular fraction, which subsequently acts as nucleation site for the remaining molecules. The phase transition temperatures and enthalpies are highly coherent with values reported in literature [ 51 ,  61 ,  62 ], especially when considering the inherent uncertainties of the heat flux calibration (e.g., the ± 1 J g −1  tolerance for the Indium reference at 10 °C min −1 ).

The reversibility of the phase transition is confirmed by the consistency between the melting enthalpies of the two heating scans. Furthermore, the crystallization enthalpies are only slightly lower than the melting ones, demonstrating that the investigated PCMs are nearly fully crystalline. These data are essential for the accurate application and performance design of TES systems, providing a reliable baseline for numerical thermal models.

sections.heading: Specific heat capacity
paragraphs: The specific heat capacity as a function of temperature was determined through DSC tests using both the sapphire method and the TOPEM ®  technique, parametrically changing the scanning rates to identify the optimum testing parameters. In the temperature window under investigation (5–90 °C), HDPE remains solid, whereas the PCMs undergo a first-order transition. The following paragraphs describe and compare the results obtained from the ASTM E1269-11 sapphire comparison and the TOPEM ®  approach.

sections.heading: Comparison with a sapphire reference
paragraphs: The effect of scanning rate on the specific heat capacity determination using the sapphire comparison can be appreciated in Fig.  3 . Fig. 3 Comparison of specific heat capacity evaluated ad different scanning rates with the sapphire method:  a  HDPE;  b  SA;  c  C20

For all materials, a pronounced increase in specific heat capacity as a function of temperature is observed, as expected. The rate of 0.1 °C min −1  yields the poorest results in terms of both precision and accuracy. This is likely due to heat dispersion and suboptimal contact with the crucible, particularly in case of HDPE, confirming that such low rates are unsuitable for DSC measurement, despite their utility in transition analysis. Conversely, as the rate increases from 1 to 10 °C min −1  a systematic shift toward higher  c p  is observed across the entire temperature range, accompanied by an increase in the error bars. While the rates within 1–10 °C min −1  provide acceptable values, the rate of 1 °C min −1  is identified as the most indicated for PCMs. It permits the most pronounced restriction of the phase transition region, while maintaining a high signal-to-noise ratio. Since 5 °C min −1  also returns sufficiently reliable values, the range of 1–5 °C min −1  is deemed suitable for determining the specific heat capacity of these organic substances.

For the PCMs (Fig.  3 b, c), a sharp increase in heat capacity and data deviation is observed, when approaching the phase transition. This evidences an incipient melting, a phenomenon where molecular mobility begins to increase before the actual melting peak is detectable in the DSC curve (Fig.  1 ). In contrast, once the liquid phase is reached, the specific heat capacity remains relatively constant, although the deviations in the liquid state are higher than in the solid state.

sections.heading: Modulated DSC–TOPEM ®
paragraphs: Figure  4  shows the results obtained through modulated DSC test using the TOPEM ®  method, which permits the direct evaluation of the specific heat capacity. In addition to HDPE and PCMs, the sapphire reference used for the ASTM E1269-11 standard was tested, and the results are compared with the values provided by the standard (Fig.  4 a). Fig. 4 Specific heat capacity evaluated with the TOPEM ®  method as function of temperature and scanning rate:  a  Sapphire;  b  HDPE;  c  C20;  d  SA

Is worth nothing that the standard deviation for the  c p  of HDPE measured at different rates is significantly higher than that of the other materials, indicating a higher sensitivity of the semi-crystalline polymer to stochastic modulation. The results for the sapphire reference evidenced that 1 °C min −1  provides more precise values than 0.3 °C min −1 , a trend confirmed for both HDPE and C20. However, the overall deviations remain high; for the SA mixture, the values converged better with the previous evaluations when adopting the slower rate of 0.3 °C min −1 . Furthermore, C20, the only material tested at 0.1 °C min −1 , yielded  c p  values statistically identical to that obtained at 1 °C min −1 . Ultimately, no clear correlation between the scanning rate-to-pulse height ratio and data stability could be established, regardless of the occurrence of melting phenomena. This underscores that further investigation and standardization are necessary for the optimization of the TOPEM ®  parameters when characterizing organic substances.

sections.heading: Specific heat capacity summary
paragraphs: The specific heat capacity values reported in literature are quite varied even for common materials like HDPE, highlighting the inherent difficulties in obtaining precise and reliable values. Karkry et al. calculated higher values for HDPE (2.05 J g −1  K −1  at 20 °C and 2.17 J g −1  K −1  at 55 °C) [ 64 ], while Ibos et al. found values statistically comparable of those reported in this paper (1.65 J g −1  K −1  at 20 °C and 2.30 J g −1  K −1  at 75 °C) adopting a scanning rate of 10 °C min −1  [ 65 ]. Recently, we evaluated 1.69 ± 0.05 J g −1  K −1  at 30 °C adopting a rate of 1 °C min −1  [ 62 ]. It is expected that the  c p  of HDPE will soar as it approaches its phase transition, similar to SA and C20, as HDPE itself can be used as a PCM [ 66 ].

Fewer data are available in literature for PCMs. Costa et al. evaluate for pure stearic acid a specific heat capacity at the liquid state (77–90 °C) of 2.59 J g −1  K −1  [ 67 ], whereas for same fatty acid mixture used here, we previously found 2.11 ± 0.09 J g −1  K −1  at 30 °C and 2.30 ± 0.11 J g −1  K −1  at 80 °C [ 51 ]. For eicosane, Kahwaj et al. reported 2.0 J g −1  K −1  at 22 °C and 2.6 J g −1  K −1  at 55 °C, declaring 10% uncertainty, results which are significantly higher than those obtained in the present study [ 68 ].

Comparing the two methods, the traditional sapphire comparison appears more precise and reliable than the TOPEM ®  technique when rates of 1–5 °C min −1  are adopted. Although the sapphire method at 5 °C min −1 , showed low internal errors, the values diverged from the theoretical values, benchmarks, suggesting that high reliability in that specific case may be coincidental. Consequently, our analysis identifies the sapphire comparison adopting a scanning rate of 1 °C min −1  as the superior method, directly challenging the ASTM E1269-11 recommendations of 20 °C min −1 . While the standard choice was likely to ensure high heat fluxes and dynamic equilibrium, modern DSC instruments have overcome these limitations. Today, the primary targets are temperature accuracy, and the reduction of the thermal inertia phenomena become the most relevant targets, both of which are best served by the 1 °C min⁻ 1  rate. This conclusion is supported by other accurate studies suggesting rates between 1 and 2.5 °C min −1  for both standard and modulated DSC characterization of organic PCMs [ 19 ,  69 ,  70 ].

As expected from previous studies [ 58 ], there is an opposite pronounced inverse relationship between thermal diffusivity and specific heat capacity. Furthermore, a significant apparent drop in thermal diffusivity in correspondence of the phase transition. However, likewise for the heat capacity, the phase transition region must be considered a zone of thermophysical indetermination; while the LFA provides numerical results in this interval, they lack physical significance due to the latent heat of fusion.

From Fig.  6 a, it is evident that LFA cross-plane measurements are highly sensitive to sample thickness, consistent with findings by Lee et al. [ 71 ]. Our results confirm that 2.5 mm is optimum thickness for HDPE to minimize the signal-to-noise ratio (S/N), as evidenced by the convergence of LFA values for 2.5 mm specimens with the independent Hot Disk results. The only discrepancy occurred at 15 °C, likely due to excessive humidity affecting the LFA sensor, as the climatic chamber was unable to effectively dehumidify the environment below 20 °C.

In literature, the thermal diffusivity of HDPE is often neglected in favor of thermal conductivity [ 72 ,  73 ], even when using direct measurement techniques like LFA [ 74 ] or Hot Disk [ 75 ], which can be considered a direct technique because the software recursively computed both thermophysical properties [ 36 ]. Ibos et al. reported values of about 0.24 mm 2  s −1  at 15 °C and 0.12 mm 2  s −1  at 80 °C for HDPE, lower than those obtained in this work; however, they also reported the higher  c p  values. Interestingly, the product of these two properties ( α · c p ) in their study remains similar to ours, suggesting that, according to Eq.  2 , the resulting thermal conductivity values are comparable assuming similar density [ 65 ]. It is critical to consider that α and λ for HDPE are heavily affected by molecular weight and chain alignment [ 76 ,  77 ].

In our previous evaluation of the same HDPE grade at 30 °C values, we obtained 0.335 ± 0.011 mm 2  s −1  via LFA and 0.294 ± 0.003 mm 2  s −1  via Hot Disk [ 62 ]. The present findings align closely with the latter, reinforcing the reliability of our optimized 2.5 mm specimen thickness.

Moving to the thermal diffusivities of the PCM, a decreasing trend is observed in the solid state (similar to HDPE), while in the liquid state the thermal diffusivity remains quite constant in the considered temperature interval; during the phase transition the obtained values can be neglected because they have no physical meaning, for analogy with the specific heat capacity, even if the producer suggests a linear interpolation from solid to liquid values to extend the validity to the phase transition. Regarding LFA holders, values obtained for solid disks were 6% to 21% lower than those obtained using the "low viscosity liquid" sample holder. While the Hot Disk results for SA converged with the low viscosity liquid holder, the results for C20 aligned better with the casted disks. These discrepancies highlight two critical technical challenges: (i) solid specimens in the Hot Disk are susceptible to improper contact at the sensor interface, and (ii) the liquid sample holder lacks sufficient volume PCM thermal expansion, potentially generating internal pressure changes or voids upon solidification. Furthermore, this sample holder intrinsically suffers of higher errors deriving from the steel plates enclosing the PCM.

For PCMs, literature data for thermal diffusivity are extremely limited, because most works reported the thermal conductivity results, even when indirectly determined. For instance, Costa et al. adopted a setup similar to that of the present work to determine the thermal conductivity of pure stearic acid, immersing the sensor within liquid state using a Transient Hot Bridge method; however, no diffusivity values were reported [ 67 ]. Kahwaji et al. detailed study the thermophysical properties trend as function of temperature of six PCMs, including eicosane. However, they reported the thermal diffusivity only at the generic solid state as 0.26 ± 0.06 mm 2  s −1 , which is fully coherent with our LFA_disk and HD values at 20–25 °C [ 68 ]. Additionally, the thermal diffusivity of SA at 30 °C (0.122 ± 0.008 mm 2  s −1  with LFA and 0.120 ± 0.012 mm 2  s −1  with Hot Disk), demonstrate high repeatability over time when compared to our previous studies [ 62 ].

Errors in the LFA test can arise as consequence of thermal expansion, since the thickness is measured at ambient temperature. Conversely, the Hot Disk method is not a strictly direct method, as accuracy can be compromised if the volumetric heat capacity ( ρ · c p ) is not precisely specified. Moreover, the long equilibrium times and limited temperature range of the Hot Disk setup (due to climatic chamber constraints) suggest that it is best utilized as a high-fidelity spot-check to validate the broader temperature sweeps provided by the LFA.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This work systematically investigated the testing methods and parameters for the thermal analysis of the first-order transitions via DSC, alongside the evaluation of specific heat capacity and thermal diffusivity. Following a comprehensive study of high density polyethylene (HDPE), selected as benchmark polymer, and two organic Phase Change Materials, (eicosane and a fatty acid mixture), the authors draw the following conclusions: The optimum DSC scanning rate for analyzing a phase transition and evaluating specific heat capacity is 1 °C min −1 , providing the most precise balance between temperature accuracy and heat flux reliability. The commonly adopted scanning rate of 10 °C min −1  causes a significant loss in temperature precision due to thermal inertia effects. Scanning rates of 0.1 and 0.01 °C min −1  permit a restricted melting temperature range but result in a systematic underestimation of the melting enthalpy. The specific heat capacity determination using the sapphire comparison gives acceptably precise and reliable values when adopting scanning rates of 1–5 °C min −1 , whereas lower speeds can generate loss in heat flux precision 1 °C min −1  is identified as the optimum scanning rate for the sapphire method, ensuring the highest reliability in temperature and heat flux determination and challenging the 20 °C min⁻ 1  recommendation of the ASTM E1269–11 standard. The specific heat capacity of organic materials strongly increases with temperature, showing a sharp rise due to incipient melting approaching the phase transition, before reaching a relatively constant value in the liquid state. The evaluation of specific heat capacity with the TOPEM ®  method yields more precise but less reliable results (higher relative error) when adopting a rate 1 °C min −1  compared to 0.3 °C min −1 . The TOPEM ®  technique requires further investigation to optimize testing parameters, such as pulse height; for HDPE, it provides results that are significantly more dispersed than those obtained with the sapphire method. Thermal diffusivity exhibits a pronounced inverse trend with temperature relative to the specific heat capacity, characterized by a sharp drop at the phase transition. LFA measurements are critically affected by the sample holder and specimen thickness, with 2.5 mm identified as suggested thickness for ensuring result convergence. Specific heat capacity and thermal diffusivity are thermophysical properties influenced by numerous experimental variables; therefore, verification of the obtained values with a second independent technique is essential for a reliable characterization.

Ultimately, the systematic protocols established in this study provide a foundation for future inter-laboratory studies aimed at standardizing advanced thermal characterization techniques for PCMs, ensuring that high-fidelity thermophysical data can be consistently reproduced across different instruments and laboratories.
